# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):

- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: All three answers make the same point, that easy access to cash and simplicity matter more than extra yield, so a finance lead would put them in one group like 'Ease and safety over yield' rather than leave each on its own, though nothing is misplaced and no group names are vague.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three speak directly to what would have made a difference.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, solution and send in a sensible order, but the window question (screen 4) sits between two context screens that carry the same heading, so the context step reads as interrupted and then restarted.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 put the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.', so it reads as being asked twice, even if each screen covers different fields.
founder.missing: Nothing asks for the price: our flat 0.25% annual fee on the balance, about $800 to $1,200 a month on a $4M to $6M reserve. Nothing asks what the team gives up today, which is mostly yield lost to the bank's treasury product (roughly $4,000 to $6,000 a month), not cash spent. Nothing asks who signs off on where the reserve sits (the founder, and often the board, an investor or a tax adviser) or about the weeks of diligence a new provider takes. The relative-advantage screen has no 'more yield' option, which is the whole point of Palus.

PRIMARY.order_why: It checks my bank first, asks about my last 3 months, then shows the idea and asks how it fits, and each follow-up comes right after the answer it asks about.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 7 overlap a little: both ask whether Palus fits how my cash is already set up, with 7 just being more specific about moving the reserve.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what matters most to me when deciding where cash sits: safety, liquidity, or operational burden versus yield. For me the burden outweighs a slightly higher rate. It also never asked roughly how much we hold or what we earn now (about 3.2% in the bank's treasury), so 'earned less than it could have' had nothing to compare against.

screens.why5: My rows are kept word for word, but the 'Keel will test' line reads 'Most finance leads they could wait two days' with a doubled subject, so my belief is garbled where it matters.
screens.why7: The picked ability row gives a balanced 2-for, 2-against scale with the escape, but the box states the bar in permission wording ('only with help or approval') while the bar line uses ability wording ('only sometimes'), and the test line doubles the subject.
screens.instead: Same three rows; Keel will test: 'Most finance leads could wait two days for their cash.' Bar: holds if no more than 1 in 3 say only sometimes, or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said how Palus fits what finance leads already do, asking what it does better than their bank's treasury is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'What does it do better than the way they do it today' is plain to me, and 'switch' is exactly how I think about moving a reserve off Mercury or Brex Treasury.
screens.why3: I know precisely what Palus beats their current setup on (yield, and not having to hire anyone to run treasury), so I can answer from my own pitch.
screens.why4: It is a free box with a single escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' fits a founder who isn't sure of their advantage.
screens.why5: The belief carries my benefit word for word: 'higher yield without hiring for treasury'.
screens.why7: The escape is right and my benefit is kept, but the card wants one benefit per row of at most 9 words while this is one 25-word box, and the belief's occasion 'their last cash decision' is the ambiguous kind the card warns about, not the monthly move where the job was at stake.
screens.instead: What does it do better than leaving the reserve in the bank's treasury? One benefit a line, up to 9 words each (e.g. 'Higher yield on the long-term reserve'), with the belief read against 'their last monthly treasury transfer'.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Palus does better, Keel shows me its draft of that benefit list and the belief it will test, so it is obvious why this screen is here.
screens.why2: Treasury and yield are my trade's own words, but 'their last cash decision' is vague to a finance lead, who would ask whether it means the monthly sweep, the post-raise placement or a vendor payment.
screens.why3: It is my own claim about my own product, worded as I gave it, so I can judge it fully.
screens.why4: The single row bundles two gains, more yield and no treasury hire, which a stranger could get one of without the other, so it should be two rows.
screens.why5: 'Higher yield without hiring for treasury' is the label I typed, kept word for word in the row and the belief.
screens.why7: The measure, the bar and the belief carrying my one benefit all fit the card, but the row bundles two gains and the occasion 'cash decision' is the ambiguous word the card names as a pitfall, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Higher yield on the reserve' · 'No treasury hire needed'; Keel will test: For most, with it, their last monthly move of reserve cash would have given them higher yield on the reserve and no treasury hire needed.

screens.why1: After what it fits with and what it does better, asking what my finance lead has to do to get going is the obvious next question about the solution.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps, learning: plain words, and the Plaid link and moving the reserve out of the bank's treasury are how I'd say it to any finance lead.
screens.why3: I know exactly what onboarding asks: link the account through Plaid, then move the long-term reserve over, and both are steps the finance lead takes themselves.
screens.why4: The box takes my efforts in my words, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right escape for a founder who isn't sure.
screens.why5: Both efforts are kept word for word, and the belief tests the one I picked, moving the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.
screens.why7: Both rows measure the extra effort to start: each is a base-form step the finance lead takes themselves, within 9 words, no sign-off and no product-side work; the belief can be supported or refuted by a yes or no to making that move; and the founder's escape is there.

screens.why1: Straight after I typed what they'll have to do, this is where I check Keel's version of the steps before picking one to test, so it's obvious why it's here.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are everyday words to a startup finance lead on Mercury or Brex, and both rows read cleanly first time.
screens.why3: Linking the bank account and moving the reserve are things the finance lead does with their own hands, so they can answer from what they actually do.
screens.why4: Both rows are distinct and in my words, but the step that really costs effort over time is missing: setting the rule that tops up the bank account from Palus each month.
screens.why5: Both rows are my own: Plaid is how we connect, and moving the reserve out of the bank's treasury is the line I wrote from 'the problem is the treasury product bundled with them'.
screens.why7: The rows are on the one measure, in shape, and each is a step the person takes; but the tested row is half a decision the founder or board makes (where the reserve sits, which is Purchase friction's ground), so a stranger's No may mean 'not my call' rather than 'too much effort', and the new monthly habit is missing.
screens.instead: Rows: Link the company bank account through Plaid · Move the long-term reserve into Palus · Set a rule to top up the bank monthly -- testing the first or third, not the reserve move.

screens.why1: After writing my efforts on the last two screens, picking the one most likely to stop a finance lead is the obvious next step before the stranger's question is set.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are everyday words to a startup finance lead and to me, and the intro says plainly what to do.
screens.why3: I know which step my finance-lead customers balk at; HN told me the treasury bundled with the bank is the real problem, not the Plaid link.
screens.why4: Both rows are my own efforts, kept word for word, distinct from each other, and the real stopper is there to pick.
screens.why5: Nothing is reworded; the belief is my own row, 'Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury', set in 'Most would ...'.
screens.why7: The rows meet the shape: two of my own base-form efforts, no Keel suggestion, the belief can go either way against yes / only if / probably not / no, and I can't tell is on the item; but the picked row bends the 'they take it themselves' rule, because in my own role split the founder decides where the reserve sits, and the row leans toward Compatibility's ground of leaving the bank's treasury.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? · Link the company bank account through Plaid · Move part of the reserve into Palus once the founder agrees · Set the rule that tops up the bank account each month

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the natural place to decide whether to collect emails from finance leads who would try it, and the founders said 'start small, try us out', so a pilot fits.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with the exact line strangers will see is plain to a founder in my position on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from the people I'm testing is my own call and I know my answer.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct, and no escape is needed for the founder's own choice.
screens.why5: My pick 'Yes' is kept and nothing about my product is changed.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out to finance leads, after the pilot offer and before sending.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says the interviewer appears 'on video' and then talks only of a 'voice', so I'm left unsure whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both, and the hint is long for a two-option pick.
screens.why3: Which interviewer my finance-lead contacts will hear is my call to make, and I can hear both samples before I decide.
screens.why4: Two distinct, named interviewers, each with a short sample, the default marked; text and tap are covered for anyone who won't talk, so no option is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my audience as 'finance leads' and alters nothing I typed about Palus.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads your questions on video? Daphne is picked for you; tap Saskia to see and hear her. (400 credits either way; people can always read and type instead.)

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, choosing how finance leads will answer is the obvious last setup step after picking who asks the questions.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'AI interviewer', 'read and tap' and 'let them choose' need no second read for a founder.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads: busy people who'd rather tap through on their own time than sit on video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete options with a sensible 'let them choose' middle; nothing missing for a format choice.
screens.why5: Nothing of mine is changed; it just addresses 'finance leads' as I typed them.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how finance leads answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words a founder uses every day: people I know, a list, one open link I post somewhere.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I'm messaging batchmates' finance leads by name or posting in a YC or founder Slack, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach finance leads (named batchmates, a searched list, one link in a group channel), and no escape is needed on a choice of method.
screens.why5: Nothing here touches what I typed about Palus; my pick, people I know by name, matches how batchmates came to us.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' carries a number, but it names Relative advantage at 2 of 6, while Adoption friction 'Did not hold' at 3 of 7 against a bar of 5 looks like the worse card, so the headline and the 'worst of all its cards' rule seem to disagree.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows its count over n and its bar, but I needed a second look to tell 'Not holding up' from 'Did not hold', and 'Adoption friction' prints two count lines.
screens.why_b3: All three dimension names and belief lines are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what to do about yield not reading as better, or about finance leads not moving the reserve out of the bank's treasury.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible, but no line says 7 is a small sample before it calls a verdict on my whole solution.
screens.instead: Not holding up: only 3 of 7 would move the reserve out of the bank's treasury (bar 5), and 2 of 6 saw a better result; with 7 people, find out first what stops them moving the cash (safety, diligence, the board).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it: 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip marks the bar at 5, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are mine word for word, but what strangers were actually asked ('would it have fitted the way things were set up for you?') drops the two days entirely, so the result is only loosely about my belief.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to Adoption friction as the real blocker is a direction, but it rests on a question that never tested the two-day wait, so I still don't know whether my liquidity claim is safe to lean on.
screens.why_b5: The So line says the two-day wait 'is not what will stop them', but no one was asked about waiting two days, only a vague 'fitted the way things were set up', so the data cannot carry that claim, even with the small-group caveat shown.
screens.instead: Ask 'On your last cash decision, could you have waited one to two business days for that cash?' and only then say whether the two-day wait holds; until then, say this screen did not test it.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside "2 of 6 said it would have gone better" and the bar, and the So line gives the deciding count: 4 of 6 against, past my limit of 2.
screens.why_b2: The Better and Same bars over 6 people read at once, but the strip puts my bar marker at 4 next to "no more than 1 in 3 say no difference or worse", which looks as if 4 against were allowed. The So line says my limit is 2 against, so I had to stop and work out that the 4 means 4 for.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and "higher yield without hiring for treasury" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and points me to the reasons. It never says what the quotes show: Dana, Marcus and Aisha would trade yield for liquidity, staying in their own bank and insured safety, so yield alone is not why finance leads would switch.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Rachel's I can't tell is set apart, and it says plainly "a small group: a lean, not a call" and "a hypothetical", so it claims nothing past these 6.
screens.instead: 4 of 6 finance leads said Palus would have made no difference, against a limit of 2. The ones who said why rank fast access, staying with their bank and safety above extra yield, so lead with those, not the rate.

screens.why_b1: 'Did not hold' sits right beside '3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short', so I know at once the reserve move is a sticking point and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 finance leads, 3 for and 4 against, with the marker at 5 of 7, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card says Adoption friction and 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury', exactly the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count, switching to 'past your bar of 2' after the header's 'bar 5 of 7'; it promises 'Their reasons are below' but the list shows only answers, with one lone quote about tax and runway, and it never says what this means for Palus, such as starting with part of the reserve.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would not move their long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury (bar: no more than 2 of 7); runway and tax worries came up, so test starting with a slice of the reserve rather than the whole of it.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Not holding up, Did not hold, Holding up) with the deciding count and bar beside it: 2 of 6 against a bar of 4, 3 of 7 against a bar of 5, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are word for word what I checked, including my own 'higher yield without hiring for treasury' label.
screens.why_b4: Beyond the 'When a line fails' header the screen never says what this means for Palus, for example that finance leads want the yield inside the bank they already use, or that the reserve-move pitch should go to founders and boards rather than finance leads.
screens.why_b5: Most counts stay visible, but the Adoption friction count line does not add up: 4 against, yet 1 asked here, 3 never saw it and 1 on Compatibility make 5; it also says Dana, Marcus and Aisha 'never saw it' when they were asked their why on Relative advantage; and single quotes stand as groups with no line saying how thin n is.
screens.why_b6: The quotes go beyond what I typed: Marcus would have taken a better rate inside his own bank, Dana pays bills straight out of treasury, Aisha has to explain any loss but never a lower yield, Rachel's accountant wants plain cash for the tax break, and Lena's board only hears 'insured'.
screens.instead: Finance leads waited the two days fine, but would not move the reserve: they value insured, explainable and inside-the-bank over yield (3 of 4 who said why). Test whether a founder or board would move it, or offer the yield without leaving their bank.

screens.why1: As the first screen it plainly checks whether my company is in the group the study is for, which is what a screener should do.
screens.why2: I'd answer it at once, but I'd pause on 'or a similar bank': Mercury and Brex are fintechs on partner banks, so I'm not sure whether a company that banks with Chase or SVB counts.
screens.why3: I run our accounts, so I know exactly where our cash sits.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but someone split across Mercury and a traditional bank, or someone whose bank is only arguably 'similar', can't tell which to pick.
screens.why5: Naming Mercury and Brex is just the segment; nothing about the founder's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with two options and is easy to answer on one hearing, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit stiff when the reply is just yes or no.
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its operating cash with Mercury, Brex or another startup-focused banking app? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury, asking whether our cash under-earned in the last quarter is the obvious next thing to check.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but 'less than it could have' makes me ask: could have compared to what, a T-bill fund, a treasury sweep, the best rate anywhere?
screens.why3: I know we earn about 3.2%, but whether that is 'less than it could have' means guessing at a benchmark nobody named, so I would guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a company or anyone's plan reaches me; it asks only about my cash.
screens.why6: One short question and 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It is on the gate's two fixed answers with no escape, but the stem is a counterfactual judgement rather than an act I did or met, and almost any treasury 'could have' earned more, so No barely has anyone left and the belief can hardly be refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you leave cash in a lower-yield account because moving it was too much work? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After asking whether our cash earned less than it could have, it's obvious why they now show me an idea for where that cash could sit.
screens.why2: Treasury account, Plaid, mortgage bonds, floating-rate, custodian and business days are all words I use running our Mercury accounts, though 'A treasury account links to...' right after naming it reads a little clumsily.
screens.why3: I decide where our raise sits and I know our sweep pays about 3.2 percent, so I can weigh this against what I actually do.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea, and the 'people building it believe' line keeps their claim as theirs rather than putting words in my mouth.
screens.why6: Six sentences in one go is a lot to hold by ear, and 'government-backed mortgage bonds, short-duration and floating-rate' is a mouthful that I'd want to hear again.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account for a startup's reserve: it links to your bank through Plaid and holds short-term, government-backed mortgage bonds in your company's name, with cash back in checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent a year, against about 3.5 percent from your bank's treasury product.

screens.why1: Right after the Palus card, asking whether it would fit how I already run cash is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: I'd have to read 'the way things were set up for you' twice: set up how, my bank, our approvals, our runway sheet, and 'cash decision' could mean anything from a sweep to a wire.
screens.why3: I know what our last cash move was, but I'd be guessing which part of our setup it is asking about, so my answer would be a guess.
screens.why4: 'Yes, most of the time' and 'Only sometimes' make no sense about one decision I made once, so two of the four labels don't fit the question.
screens.why5: Apart from the idea card shown on purpose, nothing of the founder's plan or their own words reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short and one question, and the four options and the one escape are easy to hold.
screens.why7: The condition is a vague clause rather than one whole act, the card's own pitfall, so the could-you scale has no true answer for one occasion, and the step the pitch rests on, keeping my current bank with no new operational burden, is never tested.
screens.instead: Think of your last cash decision. Could you have used it while keeping your current Mercury account? Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the fit question, asking whether it would have made things better is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: "Your last cash decision" is vague to me: I make cash calls every week (paying a vendor, moving money between accounts, where the raise sits), so I would have to reread it to work out which one is meant.
screens.why3: I know exactly how I handle our cash, but since "cash decision" could mean a routine payment or where to park the reserve, I would be half guessing which decision Palus is meant to improve.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every honest answer without overlapping, and I can't tell is the right way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan or benefits reaches me beyond the idea card I was meant to see; the options are plain better-or-worse words.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short and one question, and four short options plus one escape are easy to hold.
screens.why7: The fixed four plus I can't tell are in order and balanced, so the belief can be supported or refuted, but the occasion bends the card: "your last cash decision" is the ambiguous word the card warns about, it is not tied to a time the job of keeping raise cash safe and earning was at stake, and "go better" leaves which kind of better unclear.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you decided where your startup's cash from a raise should sit. Would Palus, a treasury account that holds a startup's reserve, have done that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: It follows straight from my answer that Palus wouldn't change much, so asking what would help instead makes obvious sense here.
screens.why2: The reference back to my answer is said the way I'd say it, but 'keeping raise cash earning better' is a knotted phrase I had to read twice; I'd say 'getting more out of our cash' or 'managing our cash'.
screens.why3: I can answer from what I do, since for us the operational burden of moving money matters more than squeezing out extra yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks beyond the name I was already shown, but 'keeping raise cash earning' is someone else's framing and assumes yield is what I care about, which drifts from how I'd put it.
screens.why6: It is one question and short enough to hear once, but 'keeping raise cash earning better' trips when spoken aloud.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't change much on your last cash decision. What would make managing your startup's cash easier or better, if anything?

screens.why1: After asking whether Palus would have helped my last cash decision, asking whether I'd actually move the reserve over is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are what I deal with every week at Mercury, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I'm the one who would move the money, so I can answer from what I'd actually do.
screens.why4: The plain 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' blurs into Yes and hides my real catch: I'd only move it if it didn't add operational work, which matters more to me than a higher yield.
screens.why5: It talks about my reserve and my bank's treasury in my own terms, and nothing beyond the idea card reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options and one escape at the end, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Moving the reserve is a step I take myself, all four fixed answers are on the one measure in order with two for and two against, the fallback label is allowed where the item has no condition, and I can't tell is the only escape.
screens.instead: To use Palus, you'd move your long-term reserve out of your bank's treasury. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it didn't add work to running our cash · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move our reserve, so asking what makes it too much trouble is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Short and clear, but 'the long-term reserve' isn't how I'd say it; I'd say 'our reserve' or 'the cash we have in treasury', and 'the' makes it sound like someone else's label.
screens.why3: I know exactly why: the operational burden of moving cash matters more to us than a bit more yield, and I deal with it every day.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: Nothing new about Palus leaks here; it only follows up on the move the last screen already put to me.
screens.why6: One short question with no list or symbols, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What makes moving your reserve out of your bank's treasury too much trouble for you?
